source_text: Credimus in caelum ascendisse, quem beatitudinis locum etiam nobis promisit, dicens: erunt sicut angeli in caelis, in illa ciuitate, quae est mater omnium nostrum Hierusalem aeterna in caelis. solet autem quosdam offendere uel inpios gentiles uel haereticos, quod credamus adsumptum terrenum corpus in caelum. sed gentiles plerumque philosophorum argumentis nobiscum agere student, ut dicant terrenum aliquid in caelo esse non posse. nostras enim scripturas non nouerunt nec sciunt quomodo dictum sit: seminatur corpus animale, surgit corpus spiritale. non enim ita dictum est, quasi corpus uertatur in spiritum et spiritus fiat, quia et nunc corpus nostrum, quod animale dicitur, non in animam uersum est et anima factum; sed spiritale corpus intellegitur, quod ita spiritui subditum est, ut caelesti habitationi conueniat, omni fragilitate ac labe terrena in caelestem puritatem et stabilitatem mutata atque conuersa. haec est inmutatio, de qua item dicit apostolus: omnes resurgemus, sed non omnes inmutabimur. quam inmutationem non in deterius, sed in melius fieri docet idem, cum dicit: et nos inmutabimur. sed ubi et quomodo sit in caelo corpus dominicum, curiosissimum et superuacaneum est quaerere; tantummodo in caelo esse credendum est. non enim est fragilitatis nostrae caelorum secreta discutere, sed est nostrae fidei de dominici corporis dignitate sublimia et honesta sentire.
thought_title: The Ascension and the Spiritual Body
orientation: Augustine is expounding the article of the creed on Christ's ascension into heaven and answering objections about an earthly body being in heaven.
pass_a_gloss: We believe that he ascended into heaven, which place of blessedness he also promised to us, saying: they will be like angels in the heavens, in that city, which is the mother of all of us, eternal Jerusalem in the heavens. But it is accustomed to offend certain people, either impious gentiles or heretics, that we believe that an earthly body was taken up into heaven. But gentiles generally strive to deal with us by the arguments of philosophers, so that they say that anything earthly cannot be in heaven. For they do not know our scriptures, nor do they know how it was said: a natural body is sown, a spiritual body rises. For it was not said in such a way, as if the body is turned into spirit and becomes spirit, because even now our body, which is called natural, has not been turned into soul and made soul; but a spiritual body is understood, which is so subjected to the spirit, that it is suited to a heavenly dwelling, with all fragility and earthly stain changed and converted into heavenly purity and stability. This is the change, about which the apostle likewise says: we will all rise, but not all will be changed. Which change the same man teaches happens not for the worse, but for the better, when he says: and we will be changed. But where and how the Lord's body is in heaven, it is most curious and superfluous to ask; only it must be believed that it is in heaven. For it is not of our fragility to examine the secrets of the heavens, but it is of our faith to think sublime and honorable things about the dignity of the Lord's body.

choices.why: Renders the Pauline contrast with 'spiritual body' in a way that keeps the physical/animal sense of 'animale' without implying it is merely animal-like.
Standard English for the Pauline phrase; keeps the noun 'body' so the contrast with 'spirit' is clear.
Keeps both nouns distinct and the adjective 'terrena' modifying 'labe' as in the Latin.
Preserves the superlative force and the two adjectives as a pair, matching Augustine's rhetorical dismissal of the question.
Keeps the neuter plural adjectives as objects of 'sentire' and the elevated register Augustine intends.

pass_b_english: We believe that he ascended into heaven, the place of blessedness that he also promised to us when he said, “They will be like the angels in heaven” (Matthew 22:30), in that city which is the mother of us all, the eternal Jerusalem in heaven (Galatians 4:26). Yet some people are usually offended—either impious Gentiles or heretics—that we believe an earthly body was taken up into heaven. The Gentiles, for the most part, try to deal with us by the arguments of the philosophers, saying that nothing earthly can exist in heaven. They do not know our Scriptures, and they do not know how it was said, “A natural body is sown; a spiritual body rises” (1 Corinthians 15:44). It was not said as if the body is turned into spirit and becomes spirit, because even now our body, which is called natural, has not been turned into soul and become soul. Rather, a spiritual body is understood as one so subjected to the spirit that it is suited to a heavenly dwelling, with all fragility and earthly stain changed and converted into heavenly purity and stability. This is the change about which the apostle also says, “We will all rise, but we will not all be changed” (1 Corinthians 15:51). He teaches that this change is not for the worse but for the better when he says, “And we will be changed” (1 Corinthians 15:52). But where and how the Lord’s body is in heaven is a most curious and superfluous question to ask; we must simply believe that it is in heaven. It is not for our fragility to examine the secrets of the heavens, but it is for our faith to think sublime and honorable things about the dignity of the Lord’s body.

last_rejected.source_quote: omnes resurgemus, sed non omnes inmutabimur
last_rejected.why: Source quotes 'resurgemus' (we will rise), matching 1 Cor 15:51 in Old Latin; but English 'We will all rise' with citation 15:51 is wrong verse. The Greek/Hebrew-numbered 15:51 reads 'we will not all sleep, but we will all be changed'—no 'rise' there. The 'rise/change' distinction Augustine quotes appears at 1 Cor 15:52 in modern numbering, or this is Old Latin 15:51. The citation should note numbering difference or use 15:52.
last_rejected.fix: 1 Corinthians 15:52 (or 15:51 in the Old Latin numbering)
last_rejected.ruling: Old Latin 'resurgemus...inmutabimur' matches 15:51 in VL numbering; citing 15:51 is standard practice for Old Latin texts.

last_rejected.why: Glossary bans 'natural' for 'animale'; 'animal' or 'animate' is required. 'Natural body' misrepresents Paul's contrast.
last_rejected.fix: An animate body is sown; a spiritual body rises
last_rejected.ruling: 'animale' rendered 'natural' is standard for 1 Cor 15:44; no glossary evidence shown, and meaning is preserved.

last_rejected.quote: The Gentiles, for the most part, try to deal with us by the arguments of the philosophers
last_rejected.source_quote: gentiles plerumque philosophorum argumentis nobiscum agere student
last_rejected.why: English loses the reported/voice marking: source has 'student' (they try), a narrative report of Gentile philosophers' position. English 'try to deal with us' makes it sound like Augustine's own statement about their activity, slightly flattening the 'reported claims' voice. But this is minor stylistic. Actually the voice is reasonably preserved. Withdrawing.
last_rejected.ruling: Checker withdrew; 'student' = 'try' is accurate; voice is preserved.
